About: Open vs Closed Pipe

Source

Topic
Standing waves in air columns — pipes open at both ends vs stopped at one end.
Concept
Stopping one end of a pipe drops the note an octave and removes every even harmonic.
Serves
NCERT Class 11 waves; JEE Physics — normal modes, harmonics, boundary conditions.
Inquiry
Predict the pitch of a closed pipe of the same length as an open one; then ask a closed pipe for its 2nd harmonic.
Misconception
"A stopped pipe must sound higher." It sounds an octave lower, because a closed pipe fits only λ/4 where an open pipe fits λ/2.

Guided Inquiry

Predict the closed-pipe note

The open pipe is sounding its fundamental. Now stop one end — same length L, but closed at the bottom. Compared to the open pipe, what note does the closed pipe sound?

Look at the drawing

Both pipes have the same length L. The closed pipe's fundamental is exactly half the open pipe's — an octave lower. The reason is drawn: the open pipe has an antinode at each end and fits half a wavelength; the closed pipe has an antinode at the open top and a node at the closed bottom, so it fits only a quarter.

Both frequencies go as 1/L, so the ratio never changes. At the closed end the air cannot move: displacement node, pressure maximum.

Does the closed pipe have an n = 2?

A pipe open at both ends has a second harmonic, n = 2, one octave above its fundamental. Does a pipe stopped at one end have one too?

The whole story

The open pipe sounds every integer multiple of its fundamental: f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, 4f₁, … The closed pipe skips every even one — n = 2, 4, 6 are not modes at all, only n = 1, 3, 5, 7, …

Two things at once, from one asymmetry (antinode ↔ node): the note drops an octave, and every even harmonic disappears. That's what makes a stopped organ pipe sound the way it does.

01

At a glance

Two air columns of the same length stand side by side. The left pipe is open at both ends. The right pipe is open at the top and closed at the bottom. The sim draws the standing wave of air in each, and the frequency each one sounds.

What you'll learn

  • How the ends of a pipe, open or closed, decide which standing waves of air fit inside it.
  • How the frequency of each mode depends on the pipe length L and the speed of sound v.
  • How displacement and pressure describe the same wave, and where each one has its nodes.
  • How to compare two pipes of the same length.
Both pipes have the same length L and an open top. Only the bottom end differs.

What's on screen

  • Open pipe (left, teal): a curve inside it is its standing wave. The frequency is printed under the pipe.
  • Closed pipe (right, amber): capped and hatched at the bottom, with its own curve and frequency.
  • N and A markers: the nodes and antinodes of the wave, with a key at the bottom of the scene.
  • L ruler: the length shared by both pipes, drawn to scale between them.
See itOpen the sim at its starting values, with both pipes sounding. Watch for: two pipes of equal length, the right one capped and hatched at the bottom, and a curve in each that moves with time.

03

An open pipe has an antinode at each end

At an open end the air is free to move, so the air displacement there is as large as it gets: a displacement antinode. In the pipe open at both ends, the waves must have an antinode at each end. Neighbouring antinodes are half a wavelength apart, so L holds a whole number of half-wavelengths:

L = n λ/2    so    fn = n v / (2L),   n = 1, 2, 3, …
Every whole number n is allowed.

With v = 343 m/s and L = 0.50 m, the open pipe gives f₁ = 343 Hz, f₂ = 686 Hz, f₃ = 1029 Hz, and so on: whole-number multiples of f₁. The n-th mode has n + 1 antinodes (A) and n nodes (N), and λ = 2L/n.

See itSet L = 0.50 m and n = 3. Watch for: the open pipe marked A at both ends with three N between, and 1029.0 Hz, λ = 0.33 m under it.
04

A closed end is a node, so only odd harmonics fit

At a closed end the air cannot move: a displacement node. The open top is still an antinode. A node and the next antinode are a quarter of a wavelength apart, so L holds an odd number of quarter-wavelengths:

L = n λ/4    so    fn = n v / (4L),   n = 1, 3, 5, …
Only odd n.
  • The fundamental has λ = 4L. At L = 0.50 m that is f₁ = 171.5 Hz, half the open pipe's 343 Hz: one octave lower.
  • An even n would need an antinode at both ends or a node at both. The closed pipe has one of each, so n = 2, 4, … do not exist.
  • The next mode above n = 1 is n = 3, at 514.5 Hz: three times f₁, not twice.
See itSet L = 0.50 m and n = 2. Watch for: the closed pipe left empty, with the message no n = 2 in a stopped pipe and next allowed mode: n = 3, while the open pipe shows 686 Hz.
05

Pressure nodes sit where displacement antinodes do

Where the air moves most, it is neither squeezed nor stretched, so the pressure change is zero there. Where the air stays still, the moving air on each side squeezes and stretches it most. Displacement and pressure describe the same wave, a quarter of a wavelength apart in space, so their nodes and antinodes swap places.

  • Open end: displacement antinode, pressure node. The air stays at outside pressure.
  • Closed end: displacement node, pressure antinode. The pressure swings the most.

The View buttons redraw the same modes. The frequencies and wavelengths do not change; only the labels N and A swap.

See itSet n = 1 and press Pressure. Watch for: the key at the bottom reading N = pressure node, with N at the top of both pipes and A at the closed bottom.
06

Both frequencies scale as 1/L

L appears only in the denominator of both formulas, so shortening a pipe raises every mode by the same factor. Halving L doubles every frequency. The ratio between the two pipes does not depend on L:

f₁(closed) / f₁(open) = (v/4L) / (v/2L) = ½
The same at every length.

Across the slider the open f₁ runs from 143 Hz (L = 1.20 m) to 858 Hz (L = 0.20 m). At L = 0.25 m the open pipe sounds 686 Hz and the closed pipe 343 Hz: the closed pipe's note at L = 0.25 m matches the open pipe's at 0.50 m.

See itSet n = 1 and shorten the pipes to L = 0.25 m. Watch for: both pipes half as tall as at 0.50 m, and 686.0 Hz under the open pipe, 343.0 Hz under the closed one.
07

Where it matters

  • Organ pipes. A stopped pipe sounds an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length, so a stopped pipe saves half the height. Its tone is hollow because it lacks the even harmonics.
  • Wind instruments. A clarinet behaves roughly like a pipe closed at one end and a flute like one open at both ends, which gives them different mixes of harmonics.
  • Resonance tube. With a tuning fork over a tube closed at the bottom, the first two resonances come at about λ/4 and 3λ/4. Their difference is λ/2, so v = 2f (L₂ − L₁) without needing the end correction.
  • Real pipes. Air just outside an open end also moves, so the effective length is slightly longer than the pipe. The sim leaves this out.
08

Summary

In one line. The ends of a pipe, open or closed, decide which standing waves of air fit inside it, and the length L and the speed of sound v decide their frequencies.

Key points

  • Open pipe: fn = n v/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … Closed pipe: fn = n v/(4L), n odd.
  • An open end is a displacement antinode and a pressure node; a closed end is the reverse.
  • At the same L, the closed pipe's fundamental is half the open pipe's, at every length.

Common mix-ups

  • "Closing an end makes the note higher." It makes the fundamental lower, because the pipe fits only a quarter-wavelength.
  • "The curve is a sideways wave." Sound in air is longitudinal. The curve shows how far the air moves along the pipe.
  • "Pressure and displacement have nodes in the same places." They are opposite: a displacement node is a pressure antinode.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the pipe length at which the closed pipe's f₁ equals the open pipe's f₁ at L = 0.50 m.
  • Set n = 5 and count the N and A markers on each pipe in the Displacement view.
